title: One Order, Door to Door

audience.who: Corporate employees in any function (sales, customer service, finance, operations support) whose work touches online orders but who never see the warehouse or the van.
audience.knows: What it is like to order online and wait; that a parcel shows status updates. Not what happens between the click and the doorstep.
audience.cares_about: Answering a customer or colleague who asks where an order is and why it is late; making promises about delivery that hold.

outcome: After watching, the viewer can trace any order through its five stations (order, pick, pack, hub sort, delivery route), name what each station does, and point to the station most likely behind a given delay before answering a customer.
through_line: An order is not one event but a relay of hand-offs, and almost every delay lives at a hand-off, so knowing the stations tells you where to look.

arc_plan.what: One customer's order placed in the evening, promised for tomorrow, and a colleague asked why it has not arrived: where would you even look?
arc_plan.source_anchor: request: topic and notes (follow one order)

arc_plan.what: By following this one order through one connected world, the viewer will be able to say what each station does and where it tends to stall.
The everyday view (click, wait, doorbell) set against the hidden chain of stations the order actually passes.

Station by station on the same map: the order is received and released to the warehouse; picked from shelves and packed; sorted at a hub onto the right outbound route; carried on a delivery route to the door. Each station: what it does, then where it can go wrong.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge sheet: order, pick and pack, hub sorting, delivery route facts

arc_plan.what: A late-order scenario with its tracking clues; the viewer decides which station most likely caused it before the answer is shown.
How to use the stations when a customer asks about an order: read the last status, name the station, set a realistic expectation.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge sheet: tracking status and delay points

arc_plan.what: Back to the opening order, now traced: the viewer can see exactly where it is and why.

must_cover.what: The order station: the order is placed, checked and released to the warehouse.
Warehouse pick and pack: items are picked from storage and packed for shipping.
Sorting at a hub: parcels are sorted toward their destination and outbound route.
The delivery route: the last stretch from the local depot to the customer's door.
Where delays usually happen, tied to the station where each occurs.
One order followed through one connected world from start to finish.

must_avoid: Statistics, percentages or timings without a source on the knowledge sheet
Naming real retailers or carriers as examples of failure
Blaming individual workers for delays; the point is the system's hand-offs
Opening by explaining terms or listing an agenda; no 'in this video we will'
Learning-styles claims and made-up sayings attributed to real people
example_posture: One fictional, ordinary order (an everyday household item) followed the whole way; every station and every delay is shown happening to that same order, never a new example per section.
visual_direction: One connected miniature world seen from above at an angle, with the stations laid out along a path the order travels; the order stays visible as the same parcel throughout; each delay shown as the parcel visibly held at a station; a few clear people at work at stations; at most a few text labels at a time.
voice_note: A capable colleague who has walked the warehouse floor explaining it over coffee: practical, calm, concrete; never lecturing, never cute about parcels.
open_questions: Topic mode, no source document: every station detail and delay cause must come from the approved knowledge sheet; the arc anchors above point to it before it exists.
Should the lesson assume a retailer running its own warehouse or a third-party carrier for the delivery route? Inferred: a generic chain covering both.
